sections.h2: Three Wickliffe offices handle every bill
sections.html:
Barlow, Kevil, La Center and Wickliffe are the four cities, and Bandana and Lovelaceville are unincorporated communities. None has its own tax office. Every Ballard County parcel is billed and managed from the courthouse area in Wickliffe.

  • Sheriff, 437 Ohio Street, Wickliffe: bills and payments, (270) 335-3561 or (270) 335-5153.
  • Property Valuation Administrator, 132 North 4th Street, Wickliffe: assessments and exemptions, (270) 335-3400.
  • County Clerk, 132 North 4th Street, Wickliffe: appeals and, later, unpaid bills, (270) 335-5168.

Wickliffe has been the county seat since 1882. A courthouse fire on February 17, 1880 burned most early records, so a buyer or heir tracing an old parcel should ask the County Clerk which books survive from before 1880.

sections.h2: When a Ballard County bill becomes late
sections.html:
KRS 134.015 supplies one schedule for every Kentucky county, and Ballard follows it unless the state allows a delay. Pay in full by November 1 and 2 percent comes off the bill. From then through December 31 you pay the printed figure. January adds 5 percent. After January the penalty is 10 percent.

A bill unpaid at the end of the day on April 15 is passed to the County Clerk, who records a lien against the parcel. From that point interest builds at 1 percent for each month, and clerk and county attorney fees are added. Under a delayed schedule each stage lasts a month, so confirm the dates with the sheriff's office.

sections.h2: The tax calendar for a Ballard County parcel
sections.html:
Property tax year at a glance
Month or windowWhat occurs
January 1Value date for real estate
January 1 to March 1Real property listing window
First Monday in May, 13 daysPublic inspection of the tax roll
Day after inspection endsLast day to file an appeal with the clerk
25 to 35 days laterLocal board hears appeals for up to five days
December 31Bills due without penalty

You needn't list the property again when last year's roll described it fully and correctly and nothing major changed. A buyer's deed price can serve as the listed value for the next January 1.

sections.h2: Paying your bill, step by step
sections.html:
Start with the Sheriff's office on Ohio Street. Ask for the current-year bill and for any balance from earlier years in the same call, because older arrears are the item that surprises sellers. If you are going to pay before November 1, confirm that the full amount must be in the sheriff's hands by that date, not just mailed.

Escrow customers should check with the mortgage servicer before paying a second time. If the servicer paid, the sheriff's record will show it. If you own the house outright, the bill is yours to pay, and 2 percent off for early payment is the best price you will see all year.

Missed December 31? Pay as soon as you can. January adds 5 percent and each later stage costs more, so a few weeks of delay does real damage. Past April 15 the County Clerk takes over, and the number you need comes from that office.

An appeal opens with a conference at the PVA's office on North 4th Street. The clerk can't take a filing otherwise. After that you have until the workday following the end of roll inspection to file with the County Clerk. Write your own opinion of value on the form, because the bill relies on it if one is printed before a decision.

  • Evidence to bring: descriptions of the land and structures, insurance policies, construction costs, nearby sales listings.
  • Anyone paid to speak for you needs recognized credentials and your written authority.
  • You may audio-record the hearing.
  • A higher value set by the board produces a supplemental bill for the difference.

Keep copies of everything you hand in. If the board's value comes back higher than yours, you'll want your own paperwork to show how you got your figure, and the hearing is audio-recorded in case anyone needs to check what was said.

An owner who never files with the local board, or files and then skips the hearing, cannot take the case to a later stage.

Owners 65 and over, or classified as totally disabled, claim Kentucky's homestead exemption through the Ballard County PVA. For 2025 and 2026 it subtracts $49,100 from the assessed value, and the amount is revisited every other year. The state runs it, not the county.

An owner who never applied might be paying tax on value the state would exempt. A call to the PVA at (270) 335-3400 settles it. Residents who are 65 or older make up a sizable share of the county, so many households could qualify.

The county sits at the far western tip of Kentucky, where the Ohio River meets the Mississippi, and the population is slowly shrinking. The 2020 count was 7,728, and the 2025 estimate is lower at 7,594. Households numbered 3,228 in 2020 and 3,209 in 2025.

The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $145,800, and owners live in 76.0 percent of occupied homes. Middle gross rent is $817 and middle household income is $66,164. The county has 3,730 housing units. With a small buyer pool, a seller whose tax account is paid up and whose deed is in order has an easier time getting to a closing. Vacancy was 12.4 percent of units at the 2020 count, so buyers have choices, and a house with open tax questions will be passed over for one without.

sections.h2: What to settle before the closing date
sections.html:
Three phone calls cover most of it. Call the Sheriff for what is owed now and in prior years. Call the County Clerk to ask whether any lien is recorded against the parcel. Call the PVA to confirm that the exemption on file, if any, is correct and that it ends properly with the sale.

If the house was in a parent's name and the paperwork never changed, sort that out first, because the County Clerk records everything and a title company will want a clean chain. Tell the clerk's office if the oldest record you need predates the 1880 fire.

sections.h2: Selling a Ballard County house when taxes are owed
sections.html:
Kentucky treats the tax as the owner's personal debt from the assessment date, and a delinquency lien, once recorded, can stay on the land for as long as eleven years whoever owns it. A closing agent therefore tends to pay the year's bill from the seller's proceeds. Ask how that year is divided with the buyer.

  • Sheriff: what is owed this year and in past years.
  • Clerk: whether a lien is on record.
  • Deed: add the next bill's mailing address, which KRS 382.135 requires.

Owners who inherited a river-county house or moved away and now owe back taxes can request a written cash offer. Any lien balance is paid out of the price.

faqs.q: Who do I pay in Ballard County?
faqs.a: Payments go to the Sheriff at 437 Ohio Street, Wickliffe. The numbers are (270) 335-3561 and (270) 335-5153.

faqs.q: How much do I save by paying early?
faqs.a: Two percent of the bill, provided the sheriff has the full amount by November 1 (KRS 134.015). After that date the printed amount stands through December 31.
The bill picks up 5 percent in January and 10 percent afterward. Once April 15 passes, the County Clerk holds it and interest of 1 percent a month runs.

faqs.q: Where is an assessment appeal filed?
faqs.a: File with the County Clerk, 132 North 4th Street, after your PVA conference. Filing closes the workday after inspection ends.

faqs.q: Is the homestead exemption a county program?
faqs.a: No, the state runs it. The Ballard County PVA, (270) 335-3400, takes applications from owners 65 or older or totally disabled, and the 2025 and 2026 amount is $49,100.
